name: bull-sleep

attributes.attribute: a divination ritual used to choose the rightful king of Tara
the Irish and Scottish name of the ritual
a king whose vision appeared to the sleeper as a naked man with birds

sources: MacCulloch, J. A. The Religion of the Ancient Celts. London: Constable, 1911, 249.
Ross, Anne. Folklore of the Scottish Highlands. London: B. T. Batsford, Ltd., 1976, 58.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The bull-sleep, also called the bull feast or tarbhfleis, is an Irish and Scottish ritual. It ranks among the great divination rites of ancient Ireland. The rite chose who would be the rightful king of Tara. A poet trained as a seer gorged on the flesh of a freshly killed bull. He then slept wrapped in its bloody hide to dream out the next king's name. Failure cost the poet his life. Some visions came out cryptic. King Conaire once appeared to the sleeper as a naked man ringed by birds. Conaire's mother was a bird. In the dream he learned to approach Tara naked, and so the prophecy came true. The Scottish Highlanders knew a like rite. They bound a diviner in bulls' hides and left him to dream of what was to come. The custom lasted long. A literary tourist in 1769 saw a solemn rite in the Trotternish district. A man was sewn into an oxhide and slept under a high waterfall to gain foreknowledge.

okr.objective: Present the bull-sleep as a divination rite that named the next king of Tara.
key_results: A poet gorged on bull flesh and slept wrapped in its bloody hide to divine the king.
